title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned The Departure Board. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Departure Board
options.lineage: Continental European station information design - SBB/DB timetable posters, split-flap boards, the Mondaine platform clock
options.thesis: Your inbox is a station concourse, not a list. Every message is a scheduled departure with a platform, a time, and a delay figure, and the board's whole job is to tell you what is late and what is boarding now. It refuses the reverse-chronological feed that every mail client ships.
options.viewport: A dense board: left a slim platform rail of the seven categories, centre the queue as timetable rows - sender, AI one-line summary, platform badge, and a right-aligned tabular delay column where overdue replies read +3d in signal red. Top-left the two-count balance, WAITING ON YOU against WAITING ON THEM, set as arrivals-white against departures-yellow. The station clock sits top-right: last sync time, its second hand pausing the way the real one does.
options.risk: Transit nostalgia. If the split-flap becomes decoration rather than the state-change itself, it reads as a theme instead of a system.

raised.raise: Colour never touches the text field. Category and priority live on the rail and the flap only; sender, subject, and summary stay achromatic ink so a dense board never becomes a carnival.

Every state is named and doubly encoded. Each of the seven categories carries a letter code and each priority a shape alongside its colour, and every board state is deep-linkable - colour is never the sole signal, and no view is unreachable by URL.
Commit is its own station. A drafted reply is staged against the original as a visible before-commit step, the way a test strip precedes the print - but reversible, because nothing here is fixer.

Focus is the primary interaction. The focused row expands in place with its full AI reading while the board steps back around it, entirely keyboard-driven - J/K walks the board, and the board never scrolls out from under you.
Handled work leaves a trace. A triaged row records its handling on the board rather than silently vanishing, and the audit log is a first-class surface, not a settings footnote.

options.label: The Strip Board
options.lineage: Air-traffic-control paper flight strips in coloured plastic holders, racked by urgency and physically moved as status changes
options.thesis: Every message is a printed strip in a coloured holder. The holder colour is the category, the rack position is the priority, and working the inbox is physically moving strips down the rack until it is clear.
options.viewport: A rack of strips, each one a fixed-height printed card in its coloured holder, ordered by consequence. Annotations are written straight onto the strip.
options.risk: It topped my own grounded list, which is exactly the warning: ranked strips in coloured holders is the most legible answer here, and legible-plus-obvious is where most runs in this category land. It also fights small screens - a rack wants width.

options.label: Emission Line Rail
options.lineage: Glass spectrogram plates on a low viewing box - a grey continuum crossed by needle-thin emission lines
options.thesis: Seven wavelengths for seven categories. Everything registers against one off-centre calibrated rail, and state is carried in line height, dash, and doubling rather than hue.
options.viewport: A charcoal plate, every message a hairline standing on the rail at its position; the urgent one doubled and standing brighter than its neighbours.
options.case: Holds product clarity - encoding state as line form rather than hue beats the board outright on colourblind legibility, and seven wavelengths for seven categories is an uncanny fit. Loses audience identification: a solo consultant triaging client mail has never read a spectrogram, and one type size ranked only by tracking risks flattening a three-pane workspace where hierarchy must land instantly.
options.risk: Single-size type across a dense app is brave until the user needs to find one thing fast.

options.label: Darkroom Safelight Bay
options.lineage: A printing darkroom under amber safelight
options.case: Fuses poorly on both axes: an amber wash over dense mail rows is a legibility problem, and its central discipline - progress irreversible past marked points - directly contradicts the product's promise that every action can be undone.
options.kept: Preview before committing, staged as its own visible station.

options.label: Iridescent Cloud Edge
options.lineage: A cloud edge diffracting sunlight into pastel bands
options.case: Loses both axes: a consultant does not identify with droplet diffraction, and colour confined to hairline edges cannot carry seven categories plus three priorities plus sentiment.
options.kept: Colour never touches the text field.

options.label: Cyclorama Dawn
options.lineage: A theatre cyclorama lit from black night through cobalt and rose into white day
options.case: Loses both axes: theatrical lighting is not the consultant's world, and stacking content into horizontal horizon bands fights a three-pane inbox at every turn.
options.kept: Named discrete states, doubly encoded and deep-linkable.

options.label: Streaming Title Wall
options.lineage: A catalog wall of horizontally scrolling poster rows
options.case: Loses both axes: it is the browse-and-graze posture, the exact opposite of triage, and poster tiles carry no data because email has no artwork.
options.kept: Focus expands in place while the surround dims.

options.label: Flash Scrawl Club Sleeve
options.lineage: A French house label sleeve defaced with marker scrawl
options.case: Loses both axes by a distance: nothing about a consultant's client correspondence lives in club ephemera, and scrawl over dense tabular data is unreadable.
options.kept: Used controls stay on the surface as history.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: The Linear/Superhuman rendition, executed impeccably: near-black or off-white ground, one grotesque, hairline borders, a single violet accent, rounded cards, generous whitespace, tiny muted labels.
canonCard.viewport: The three-pane inbox a visitor already expects, at full craft.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every other AI inbox tool by design.
